d.t: The name of the letter Y.
d.e: The names of the letters, as now commonly spoken and written in English, are A, Bee, Cee, Dee, E, Eff, Gee, Aitch, I, Jay, Kay, Ell, Em, En, O, Pee, Kue, Ar, Ess, Tee, U, Vee, Double-u, Ex, Wy, Zee.

d.t: A member of a Native American people, formed from the Huron confederacy, that lived in and around Ohio.
A member of the Wyandotte people.

d.e: The adaptable Harris picked out Mr. Carrados's most substantial rug and went to sleep, to dream of a wayside cycle shop and tea-rooms where he could devote himself to pedigree Wyandottes.

d.t: The name of the Latin script letter Y/y.
d.e: Thus first C checks to see if ex and wye are equal. The resulting value of 1 or 0 (true or false) then is compared to the value of zee.

d.t: A Y-shaped object: a wye level, wye-connected. Especially a Y-shaped connection of three sections of road or railroad track.
d.e: A wye is used to split a single line [hose or cable] into two lines.

d.t: To make something into a wye (letter Y) shape.
d.e: When a hose line is divided into two or more lines, these lines are known as wyed lines.

d.t: To reverse the direction of a train using a wye.
d.e: Since the train didn't have a control cab at the other end, they wyed the train to turn it around for the trip back to the city.

d.t: A narrow lane, alley or path, especially one between houses.
d.e: Fortune favoured us, and we got home without meeting a soul. Once we saw a man, who seemed not quite sober, passing along a street in front of us; but we hid in a door till he had disappeared up an opening such as there are here, steep little closes, or wynds, as they call them…

This was then used as the base for the cocks of hay, or wyndes as we called them. […] A piece of hay with its ends firmly embedded in the base of the wynde was wound around the hay twine and knotted with it. The ball of twine was then thrown across the wynde and tied at the other…

d.t: A letter of the Old English alphabet, ƿ, borrowed from the futhark and used to represent the sound of w; replaced in Middle English times by the digraph uu, which later developed into the letter w.
d.e: The Norman scribes gradually replaced wynn by u, uu, vv, and w itself.

d.t: Fate, destiny, particularly in an Anglo-Saxon or Old Norse context.
d.e: Wyrd is too vast, too complex for us to comprehend, for we are ourselves part of wyrd and cannot stand back to observe it as if it were a separate force.

d.t: A huge limbless and wingless dragon or dragonlike creature.
A type of software that maintains a close correspondence between the screen image and the printed image.
d.e: WYSIWYGs are helpful tools in that they enable you to create pages much more quickly

d.t: A continuous vertical section of masonry, one unit in thickness.
d.e: That wall has to be at least three wythes of brick to support your load.

d.t: A partition between flues in a chimney.
d.e: A chimney runs from the base of the first flue liner to the top of the last flue liner, or to any rain cap above it. Attach single-wythe chimneys to the house.

d.t: A draconian creature possessing wings, only two legs and usually a barbed tail.
